About: polarisation of a plane wave as the path of the tip of E at one point

About this simulation

On screen
Left: the Ex–Ey plane at z = 0, seen facing the oncoming wave, on equal scales from −1200 to +1200 V/m. It shows the field arrow, the fading trail of its tip over the last period and a dashed rectangle at Ex = ±E1, Ey = ±E2. Right: Ex (solid) and Ey (dashed) against t/T over one period, with a cursor at the present instant.
Controls
E1 and E2 set the amplitudes of the x- and y-components, 0 to 1000 V/m. ψ sets the phase difference, −π to π in steps of π/12. Every change restarts the clock at t = 0 and clears the trail. Play and pause run the slowed clock.
Measured
The Readouts panel gives t/T, Ex, Ey and |E| at the present instant: Ex = E1 cos ωt and Ey = E2 cos(ωt − ψ), evaluated from the plane-wave field op. The magnitude is |E| = √(Ex² + Ey²). The motion is slowed to one period T every 4 s. In free exploration a second group gives the path over one period: its largest and smallest |E| (the half-lengths of the ellipse), the tilt of its long axis from x, and the sense in which the tip goes round, seen facing the oncoming wave.

Guided Inquiry

1 · In step

Set E1 and E2 to 800 V/m and ψ to 0, with the simulation paused at t = 0, so that the arrow points to the corner of the dashed square. Before pressing play, predict the path the tip will trace.

2 · A quarter period apart

Keep E1 and E2 at 800 V/m, press pause, and set ψ to π/2 (the readout shows 0.50π). Before pressing play, predict the path and the sense in which the tip moves along it.

3 · The other sign

Keep E1 and E2 at 800 V/m, press pause, and set ψ to −π/2 (the readout shows −0.50π). Before pressing play, predict what changes.

4 · An eighth of a period apart

Keep E1 and E2 at 800 V/m, press pause, and set ψ to π/4 (the readout shows 0.25π). Before pressing play, predict the path.

5 · Three eighths of a period apart

Keep E1 and E2 at 800 V/m, press pause, and set ψ to 3π/4 (the readout shows 0.75π). Before pressing play, predict the path.

6 · Unequal amplitudes

Press pause and set E1 to 800 V/m, E2 to 400 V/m and ψ to π/2 (the readout shows 0.50π). Before pressing play, predict the path.

7 · Summary

The tip of E at one point traces an ellipse. The phase difference ψ between Ex and Ey decides its shape: ψ = 0 or π gives a straight line (linear polarisation), and ψ = ±π/2 with E1 = E2 gives a circle.

The sign of sin ψ decides the sense: positive ψ turns the field anticlockwise, seen facing the oncoming wave, and negative ψ clockwise. The Path readouts now give the half-lengths, tilt and sense for any setting.

The Physics

The Tip of the Electric Field · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim follows the tip of the electric field of a plane wave at one point, built from an x-component and a y-component of one frequency. You set the two amplitudes and the phase difference between them.

What you'll learn

  • How the path of the tip depends on E1, E2 and ψ.
  • What fixes the direction in which the tip goes round.
  • What the Largest |E|, Smallest |E| and Tilt readouts measure.
The set-up, facing the oncoming wave: the field E at one instant and its two components. The dashed rectangle marks ±E1, ±E2.

What's on screen

  • Left canvas, cyan: the field arrow and the fading trail of its tip over the last period.
  • Blue dot on the Ex axis and violet dot on the Ey axis: the two components now.
  • Dashed rectangle: Ex = ±E1 and Ey = ±E2.
  • Right plot: Ex (solid blue) and Ey (dashed violet) against t/T, with a cursor at now.
  • Readouts: the field now, then the path over one period.
See itLook at the starting scene before the arrow moves. Watch for: the arrow at t = 0, the two dots on the axes, and the right plot with its cursor at the left edge.

03

The tip traces a line, a circle or an ellipse

Two plane waves of one frequency add to another solution. At z = 0 the components are Ex = E1 cos ωt and Ey = E2 cos(ωt − ψ) (notes, 9.24). The tip of the sum goes round a closed curve once per period.

If ψ = 0 the components rise and fall together, Ey/Ex stays at E2/E1, and the tip moves back and forth along a straight line: linear polarisation. At the opening 800 and 800 V/m it is the diagonal, and |E| reaches 1131 V/m at the corners.

If E1 = E2 = E0 and ψ = π/2, then Ex = E0 cos ωt and Ey = E0 sin ωt (9.25). |E| = E0 at every instant and the tip goes round a circle: circular polarisation. ψ = ±π, or a zero amplitude, also gives a line; every other setting gives an ellipse.

The path over one period at E1 = E2 = 800 V/m, as in notes Fig. 94. The dashed square is ±E1, ±E2. Arrows: direction of travel.
See itPlay ψ = 0 at E1 = E2 = 800 V/m (all three are set for you). Watch for: the arrow swinging back and forth along the diagonal, with |E| rising from 0 to 1131 V/m and back.
04

The sign of ψ sets the direction the tip goes round

Look at the field a quarter period after t = 0, facing the oncoming wave with x to the right and y up. At ωt = π/2, Ex = 0 and Ey = E2 sin ψ. For ψ = π/2 the field has swung from along +x to along +y, so the tip turns anticlockwise.

For ψ = −π/2 the same quarter period leaves E along −y, and the tip turns clockwise. The circle is the same.

The tip at t = 0 (black) and at t = T/4 (amber), E1 = E2 = E0.
Key idea. For every ellipse, 0 < ψ < π gives anticlockwise and −π < ψ < 0 gives clockwise (notes, Problem 2). It is the sign of sin ψ that decides. At ψ = 0 and ψ = π, sin ψ = 0 and the path is a line with no sense.

The notes state the sense explicitly, because left-circular and right-circular are attached to the two senses in opposite ways in different parts of physics.

See itPlay ψ = π/2 at 800 and 800 V/m. After about 6 s ψ is set to −π/2. Watch for: the Sense readout changing from anticlockwise to clockwise while the circle and |E| stay the same.
05

The Largest and Smallest |E| are the half-lengths of the ellipse

Eliminating t with 𝒳 = Ex/E1 and 𝒴 = Ey/E2 gives the path:

𝒳² − 2𝒳𝒴 cos ψ + 𝒴² = sin²ψ
Equation (9.27). An ellipse centred on the origin whenever sin ψ ≠ 0.

The Largest |E| and Smallest |E| readouts are its half-lengths, and the Tilt readout is the angle of its long axis from x. At 800 and 800 V/m with ψ = π/4 they are 1045 and 433 V/m, with the long axis along Ey = Ex.

The notes’ axes 𝒴 = ±𝒳 hold in the scaled variables only. With unequal amplitudes the long axis is not along the rectangle’s diagonal. For ψ = ±π/2 the axes lie along x and y: 800 and 400 V/m give an untilted ellipse, 800 V/m along x and 400 V/m along y.

E1 = 1000 V/m, E2 = 500 V/m, ψ = π/4.
E1 E2 ψ

These sliders move the sim too. The numbers come from the sim’s own function.

See itPlay E1 = 1000 V/m, E2 = 500 V/m, ψ = π/4 (all three are set for you). Watch for: the long axis tilted 22° from x, flatter than the rectangle’s 27° diagonal.
06

ψ and −ψ give the same ellipse, traced in opposite senses

The path (9.27) contains ψ only through cos ψ and sin²ψ. Changing ψ to −ψ alters neither, so the ellipse is the same. What changes is sin ψ, which only the motion along the path remembers. That is the sense.

The notes rewrite the left side as (𝒳 − 𝒴 cos ψ)² + 𝒴² sin²ψ, so in the variables 𝒳 − 𝒴 cos ψ and 𝒴 sin ψ the path is a circle of radius |sin ψ|.

Changing ψ to π − ψ flips the sign of cos ψ and keeps sin ψ. At 800 and 800 V/m, ψ = 3π/4 gives the π/4 ellipse again, 1045 by 433 V/m, with its long axis now along Ey = −Ex. sin ψ is still positive, so it is still anticlockwise.

E1 = E2 = 800 V/m. The two ellipses are mirror images in the y-axis.
See itPlay ψ = π/4 at 800 and 800 V/m. After about 6 s ψ is set to 3π/4. Watch for: Tilt of long axis changing from 45° to −45° while Largest |E|, Smallest |E| and Sense stay put.
07

The energy density pulses for linear light and holds steady for circular light

A plane wave carries equal electric and magnetic energy, so its energy density is u = ε0|E|² (9.29). The |E| readout is therefore a gauge of u.

For linear polarisation |E| swings between 0 and its peak, and u does so twice per period. For circular polarisation |E| = E0 at every instant, so u = ε0E0² does not change.

u through one period for E1 = E2 = 800 V/m. The linear curve averages the circular value.

The average is the same for both. Since ⟨Ex²⟩ = E1²/2 and ⟨Ey²⟩ = E2²/2, ⟨u⟩ = ε0(E1² + E2²)/2 for every ψ. The intensity is ℐ = c⟨u⟩ (9.33), which is 1.70 kW/m² at 800 and 800 V/m (9.34).

See itPlay ψ = 0 at 800 and 800 V/m. After about 6 s ψ is set to π/2. Watch for: |E| swinging between 0 and 1131 V/m, then holding at 800 V/m.
08

Where it matters

  • Polarising filters. An ideal filter passes the component of E along its transmission axis. Linearly polarised light of intensity ℐ0 at an angle θ to the axis comes out with ℐ = ℐ0 cos²θ, Malus’s law (notes, 9.35).
  • Unpolarised light. The Sun and a filament lamp emit from countless atoms acting independently. Their polarisation changes at random, far faster than detectors respond, and the light is unpolarised (notes).
  • Naming the sense. “Left” and “right” circular are attached to the two senses in opposite ways in different parts of physics, so state the sense, as the Sense readout does.
09

Summary

In one line. The sim shows the path that the tip of an electric field traces at one point, for two components whose amplitudes and phase difference you choose.
  • ψ = 0 or ±π (or one amplitude zero) gives a line, E1 = E2 with ψ = ±π/2 a circle, anything else an ellipse (9.27).
  • The sign of sin ψ sets the sense: anticlockwise for ψ > 0, clockwise for ψ < 0.
  • The mean energy density, ε0(E1² + E2²)/2, does not depend on ψ.

Common mix-ups

  • "Equal amplitudes make a circle." Only with ψ = ±π/2. With ψ = 0 the same 800 and 800 V/m give a straight line.
  • "ψ = π/2 always makes a circle." It needs E1 = E2 too. 800 and 400 V/m give an untilted ellipse.
  • "Past π/2 the tip reverses." The sense flips only where sin ψ changes sign, at 0 and π.

Things to try on your own

  • Set E1 = 0 and E2 = 500 V/m. Vary ψ and watch the path and Sense.
  • At ψ = π/2 double both amplitudes from 400 to 800 V/m. Compare the radius and the energy density.
  • Compare ψ = π/4 and −π/4 at 800 and 800 V/m, and name what is the same and what differs.
